lesson.title: The Small Loops That Solve Everything: Mesh Current Analysis
lesson.summary: A mesh is a loop that encloses no other loops inside it, and assigning a circulating current to each mesh turns Kirchhoff's Voltage Law into a compact, solvable system of equations.
lesson.body:
A mesh is a special kind of loop: it is a loop that has no other loop, and no other branch, inside it. This definition only makes sense for planar circuits, ones that can be drawn on a flat page without any wires crossing, because "inside" only means something once the circuit has a clear picture with regions enclosed by branches. In the three branch circuit from the previous chapter, the loop formed by branch 1 and branch 2 is a mesh, and the loop formed by branch 2 and branch 3 is a mesh, but the outer loop formed by branch 1 and branch 3 is not a mesh, because branch 2 sits inside the region that loop encloses. Every mesh is a loop, but not every loop is a mesh.

Meshes matter because they give you a systematic, non redundant way to pick independent loops. Instead of writing a KVL equation for a branch current in every branch, you assign one circulating mesh current to each mesh, and let that single unknown represent the current flowing all the way around that mesh's boundary. Where two meshes share a branch, the actual current through that shared branch is simply the difference of the two adjacent mesh currents. This cuts the number of unknowns down to the number of meshes, which is usually far fewer than the number of branches, and it automatically satisfies KVL and KCL together.

Reuse the two node, three branch circuit from before: branch 1 has a 10V source in series with a 2 ohm resistor R1, branch 3 (the shared middle branch) is a 4 ohm resistor R3, and branch 2 is a 2 ohm resistor R2 with no source. This defines two meshes. Let I1 be the clockwise mesh current in the left mesh (through R1 and R3), and I2 the clockwise mesh current in the right mesh (through R3 and R2). Writing KVL around mesh 1: negative 10V, plus I1 times 2 ohm, plus (I1 minus I2) times 4 ohm, equals zero, which simplifies to 6I1 minus 4I2 equals 10. Writing KVL around mesh 2, which has no source of its own: (I2 minus I1) times 4 ohm, plus I2 times 2 ohm, equals zero, which simplifies to 6I2 minus 4I1 equals zero, or I2 equals two thirds of I1.

Substituting I2 equals two thirds of I1 into the first equation gives 6I1 minus 4 times two thirds of I1 equals 10, which reduces to 10 divided by 3, times I1, equals 10, so I1 equals 3A exactly. Then I2 equals two thirds of 3A, or 2A exactly. The actual current through the shared resistor R3 is I1 minus I2, which is 3A minus 2A, or 1A. Checking mesh 1: negative 10, plus 2 times 3, plus 4 times 1, equals negative 10 plus 6 plus 4, equals zero. Checking mesh 2: 4 times (2 minus 3), plus 2 times 2, equals negative 4 plus 4, equals zero. Both check out exactly.

Notice that mesh 2 has no independent source of its own, yet it still carries a full 2A, purely because it is coupled to mesh 1 through the shared resistor R3. That coupling is precisely why you cannot solve the two meshes one at a time, you have to solve them together as a system. This same pattern, one KVL equation per mesh, solved simultaneously, extends directly to circuits with three, four, or more meshes, and it is the standard method for finding branch currents throughout any planar resistive network.
